blocks.content:
Evaluating medical treatments requires collecting structured data rather than relying on individual anecdotes or expectations. To determine whether an intervention produces real benefits, researchers set up an experiment with two main comparison sets: a **treatment group** that receives the intervention alongside standard care, and a **control group** that receives only standard care as a reference point.

Because looking at raw data patient by patient is unwieldy, researchers calculate summary statistics. A **summary statistic** is a single number that summarizes a large amount of raw data. Comparing summary statistics across groups reveals whether the treatment produced an effect and helps researchers evaluate if the difference is larger than what would occur by pure chance.

Consider an experiment designed to test whether stents reduce stroke risk in at-risk patients. Researchers randomly assigned 451 patients into two groups: 224 patients to the treatment group (stent plus medical management) and 227 patients to the control group (medical management only). After one year, researchers recorded stroke outcomes:
1. In the treatment group, 45 out of 224 patients suffered a stroke. Dividing 45 by 224 yields a stroke proportion of 0.20, or 20%.
2. In the control group, 28 out of 227 patients suffered a stroke. Dividing 28 by 227 yields a stroke proportion of 0.12, or 12%.
3. Subtracting the control group rate from the treatment group rate (20% - 12%) shows that an additional 8% of patients in the treatment group experienced a stroke.

Contrary to expectations, patients receiving stents had a higher stroke rate. This demonstrates the crucial insight that data analysis must remain open to surprising findings rather than assuming a medical intervention will succeed.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A control group provides a reference point for measuring the impact of a medical treatment.
A summary statistic is a single number that summarizes a large amount of raw data.
In the stent study, 20% of treatment patients had a stroke at 1 year compared to 12% of control patients.
Data analysis allows researchers to evaluate whether observed differences are larger than expected by chance.

blocks.content:
When working with real-world information, raw data can quickly become chaotic and difficult to analyze. To solve this problem, statisticians and data scientists organize information into a standardized rectangular layout called a **data matrix**.

In a standard data matrix, each row represents an individual **case** or **observational unit**, which is the single subject or object being measured. Each column represents a **variable**, which is a specific characteristic recorded for every case. Organizing data in this grid structure makes it easy to append new observational units as additional rows or measure new attributes by adding columns.

Consider the `loan50` dataset, which records financial information for loans from Lending Club. As shown in Figure 1.3, the table organizes 50 randomly selected loans. In row 1, the observational unit is a single loan. Reading across the columns for row 1, we observe seven specific variables: a `loan amount` of $7,500, an `interest rate` of 7.34%, a `term` of 36 months, a loan `grade` of A, the borrower's `state` of MD (Maryland), a `total income` of $70,000, and a `homeownership` status of rent. Row 2 represents a completely separate case—a $25,000 loan with a 9.43% interest rate for a borrower in Ohio earning $254,000 with a mortgage.

The point to take from it is that one row is one observation, one person's loan, and each position along the row is a different variable measured on that same person. blocks.content: The essential insight to remember is that every row in a data matrix corresponds to a unique case, while every column corresponds to a variable.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A data matrix is a standard rectangular structure for organizing datasets.
Each row in a data matrix represents a unique case or observational unit.
Each column in a data matrix corresponds to a single variable.
New measurements for subjects are recorded by adding rows, while new characteristics add columns.

blocks.content:
When working with raw data, researchers need a structured framework to organize, analyze, and visualize information effectively. Data sets are typically arranged in tables where each row represents a distinct observation or case, and each column represents a **variable**, which is a characteristic recorded for each case.

As shown in **Figure 1.7**, variables fall into two main categories: **numerical** and **categorical**. Numerical variables take numerical values where arithmetic operations like addition or averaging are meaningful. A numerical variable is **discrete** if it takes integer counts with distinct jumps, such as population counts. Conversely, it is **continuous** if it can take any fractional value along a continuum, such as unemployment rates or student heights. Categorical variables classify observations into distinct groups called **levels**. If these levels have a natural ranking, such as education levels, the variable is **ordinal**; if no natural ordering exists, such as state names or experimental treatment groups, it is **nominal**.

blocks.title: Figure 1.7
blocks.caption: Breakdown of variables into their respective types.
blocks.alt: Figure 1.7: Breakdown of variables into their respective types.
blocks.description: A tree diagram that sorts every variable into a type. The box at the top reads "all variables" and splits into two branches, "numerical" on the left and "categorical" on the right. Numerical splits again into "continuous" and "discrete". Categorical splits into "nominal (unordered categorical)" and "ordinal (ordered categorical)", both drawn in grey to mark them as the finer distinction. The takeaway is the decision order: first ask whether a variable is a number you can do arithmetic on or a label; if a number, ask whether it can take any value in a range (continuous) or only separated values such as whole counts (discrete); if a label, ask whether the categories have a natural order (ordinal) or not (nominal).

blocks.content:
To illustrate this classification process, consider a study evaluating a migraine treatment. Researchers record two variables for each patient: `group` (with values *treatment* or *control*) and `num_migraines` (the number of migraines experienced over a three-month period).

1. For `group`, the values are non-numerical labels (*treatment* or *control*), and arithmetic operations cannot be performed on them. Therefore, `group` is classified as a **categorical variable** (specifically nominal).
2. For `num_migraines`, the recorded values represent counts of discrete events ($0, 1, 2, \dots$). Basic arithmetic like calculating the mean number of migraines is sensible, and values proceed in integer jumps rather than a continuous spectrum. Thus, `num_migraines` is classified as a **discrete numerical variable**.

Understanding the exact type of each variable is essential because it determines which statistical summaries and graphical tools, such as scatterplots, are appropriate for analyzing relationships.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Data tables structure information with rows representing individual cases and columns representing variables.
Numerical variables can be discrete (counts with integer jumps) or continuous (values along a continuum).
Categorical variables describe qualitative levels and can be nominal (unordered) or ordinal (naturally ordered).
Variables are considered associated or dependent when a discernible pattern exists between them.

blocks.content:
When researchers explore relationships between variables, they often need a structured way to describe which variable acts as the potential cause and which acts as the outcome. Without clear definitions, it is difficult to formulate specific hypotheses about how variables interact.

To solve this, researchers designate roles for the variables based on their underlying hypotheses. When we suspect that one variable might causally affect another, we label the suspected driver as the **explanatory variable** and the outcome as the **response variable**. If two variables show a clear trend together, they are described as **associated**. When a higher value in one variable corresponds to a higher value in another, they are positively associated, whereas an inverse trend indicates negative association. Conversely, if no relationship exists between two variables, they are considered **independent**.

Consider a study examining county-level data between 2010 and 2017. Researchers evaluate two variables: median household income and population change. If researchers ask whether an increase in median household income drives an increase in a county's population, they identify median household income as the explanatory variable and population change as the response variable. Data from this period shows that counties with higher median household incomes generally experienced higher population growth rates, demonstrating a positive association.

However, simply labeling variables as explanatory and response does not guarantee that a causal relationship exists. Observational studies can show that variables are associated, but proving true causation requires conducting a randomized experiment.

blocks.title: Explanatory vs response variables
blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 240" width="760" height="240"><defs><marker id="ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#9ca3af"/></marker></defs><g font-family="ui-sans-serif,system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#e5e7eb"><rect x="24" y="36" width="280" height="168" rx="8" fill="#1f2937" stroke="#4b5563"/><text x="40" y="64" fill="#6366f1" font-weight="bold" font-size="14">Explanatory Variable (X)</text><text x="40" y="88" fill="#9ca3af" font-size="12">The suspected cause or driver</text><rect x="40" y="104" width="248" height="36" rx="4" fill="#111827" stroke="#4b5563"/><text x="164" y="127" text-anchor="middle" fill="#e5e7eb">Median Household Income</text><path d="M316,120 H380" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ar)"/><text x="348" y="110" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9ca3af" font-size="11">predicts</text><rect x="392" y="36" width="280" height="168" rx="8" fill="#1f2937" stroke="#4b5563"/><text x="408" y="64" fill="#22c55e" font-weight="bold" font-size="14">Response Variable (Y)</text><text x="408" y="88" fill="#9ca3af" font-size="12">The measured outcome or effect</text><rect x="408" y="104" width="248" height="36" rx="4" fill="#111827" stroke="#4b5563"/><text x="532" y="127" text-anchor="middle" fill="#e5e7eb">Population Growth Rate</text><text x="164" y="176" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9ca3af" font-size="12">Plotted on Horizontal Axis</text><text x="532" y="176" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9ca3af" font-size="12">Plotted on Vertical Axis</text></g></svg>
blocks.caption: The explanatory variable is treated as the proposed driver on the horizontal axis, while the response variable measures the resulting outcome on the vertical axis.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The **explanatory variable** is the variable suspected of affecting the outcome, while the **response variable** measures that outcome.
Two variables are **associated** if a relationship exists between them, and **independent** if no evident relationship exists.
A pair of variables can be either associated or independent, but never both at the same time.
Labeling a variable as an explanatory variable does not guarantee that a true causal relationship exists.

blocks.content:
When researchers want to answer broad questions about large groups, measuring every single individual object or person—known as a **case**—is usually impossible or far too expensive. For instance, measuring the mercury content of every single swordfish residing in the Atlantic Ocean would be completely impractical.

To solve this challenge, researchers distinguish between a broad **target population** and a manageable **sample**. The population encompasses all possible cases of interest, such as all swordfish in the Atlantic Ocean. Because testing the entire population is unfeasible, researchers collect a sample, which is a small subset of the population (for example, measuring a sample of 60 selected swordfish). By analyzing the data gathered from these 60 fish, statisticians can estimate the average mercury concentration for the entire Atlantic swordfish population.

A common mistake when answering statistical questions is relying on **anecdotal evidence**. This occurs when individuals draw general conclusions from haphazardly collected data or extraordinary isolated incidents. For example, a person might hear a news report about one individual who contracted mercury poisoning after eating swordfish and conclude that average mercury levels in all swordfish must be dangerously high. This reasoning is flawed for two distinct reasons: first, the conclusion relies on data from only one or two cases; second, and more critically, extraordinary cases collected casually are rarely representative of the broader population. As illustrated by weather events like a single massive snowstorm (as discussed alongside Figure 1.10), one isolated observation in a single region does not disprove a long-term global pattern. To make reliable scientific statements, researchers must collect representative samples comprising many cases rather than relying on striking, memorable exceptions.

blocks.caption: In February 2010, some media pundits cited one large snow storm as valid evidence against global warming. As comedian Jon Stewart pointed out, “It’s one storm, in one region, of one country.”
blocks.alt: Figure 1.10: In February 2010, some media pundits cited one large snow storm as valid evidence against global warming. As comedian Jon Stewart pointed out, “It’s one storm, in one region, of one country.”

It is a chapter-section opening photograph and carries no data, no axes and nothing to read off; it sets a scene for the sampling discussion rather than illustrating a result. Nothing in the lesson's argument depends on it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A target population consists of all the individual cases of interest for a research question.
A sample is a smaller subset of cases drawn from the population to estimate broad trends.
Anecdotal evidence relies on haphazardly collected data from just one or two unusual cases.
Casual observations are often unrepresentative because memorable or extraordinary events stand out in memory.
Proper statistical conclusions require systematic sampling across many representative cases.

blocks.content:
When researchers want to understand a large group, collecting data from every single individual is often impossible or impractical. To solve this, statisticians select a smaller subset called a **sample** to represent the target **population**. However, choosing individuals by hand or relying on easily reachable people can introduce **bias**, making the sample unrepresentative.

To prevent unintentional bias, we use random selection. In a **simple random sample**, every case in the population has an equal chance of being selected, similar to drawing tickets from a raffle. Even with random sampling, challenges such as **non-response bias** (when selected individuals do not participate) or reliance on a **convenience sample** (sampling only easily accessible individuals) can corrupt the findings.

Furthermore, researchers must consider data collection types. In **observational studies**, researchers collect data without applying any treatment. While these studies can identify associations, they cannot establish causal relationships because of potential **confounding variables**—unmeasured factors correlated with both the explanatory and response variables.

Consider an observational study tracking sunscreen usage and skin cancer rates. Suppose the study finds that individuals who use more sunscreen also have higher rates of skin cancer. It would be incorrect to conclude that sunscreen causes skin cancer. The missing factor in this scenario is sun exposure. A person spend hours in the sun is both more likely to apply sunscreen and more likely to develop skin cancer. Here, sun exposure acts as a **confounding variable** that explains the observed link between sunscreen use and skin cancer.

The key insight to remember is that random sampling minimizes selection bias, and observational studies reveal associations rather than direct causation.

blocks.caption: Examples of simple random and stratiﬁed sampling. In the top panel, simple random sampling was used to randomly select the 18 cases. In the bottom panel, stratiﬁed sampling was used: cases were grouped into strata, then simple random sampling was employed within each stratum.

blocks.description: Two stacked panels showing the same set of individuals sampled two different ways. The top panel is a plain rectangle with roughly a hundred blue dots scattered at random across it; about eighteen of them are circled in red, spread evenly over the whole rectangle with no pattern. That is a simple random sample. The bottom panel contains the same rectangle but the dots are gathered into six labelled groups, Stratum 1 through Stratum 6, drawn as circles of different sizes; inside every stratum two or three dots are circled in red. That is a stratified sample. The comparison to take away: the simple random sample lets the draws fall where they may and can happen to miss a group, while the stratified design first divides the population into similar groups and then deliberately samples from within each one, guaranteeing every stratum is represented.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A sample is a subset selected to represent an entire target population.
Simple random sampling gives every case an equal chance of selection to reduce bias.
Convenience sampling and high non-response rates introduce bias into sample results.
Observational studies can show associations but cannot prove causal relationships.
Confounding variables correlate with both explanatory and response variables, obscuring true causes.

blocks.content:
When researchers collect data from large or geographically dispersed populations, standard simple random sampling can become prohibitively expensive and logistically difficult. Advanced sampling strategies solve this problem by organizing the population into subgroups before selecting individuals, balancing precision against data collection costs.

**Stratified sampling** is a divide-and-conquer strategy where the population is divided into homogeneous groups called **strata**. Because cases within each stratum are chosen to be very similar with respect to the outcome of interest, sampling within strata produces highly stable estimates for each subpopulation. When these estimates are combined, the overall population estimate becomes much more precise. For instance, in professional baseball, teams can serve as strata because player payrolls vary widely across teams (up to 4 times as much). If a researcher samples 4 players randomly from each of the 30 teams, the resulting sample size is $30 \times 4 = 120$ players. This guarantees representation across all teams while improving estimation precision.

Conversely, **cluster sampling** and **multistage sampling** divide the population into diverse groups called **clusters**. In cluster sampling, researchers randomly select a subset of clusters and include every observation inside those chosen clusters. In multistage sampling, researchers randomly select a subset of clusters and then take a secondary random sample of observations within each selected cluster, as Figure 1.15 shows. Consider estimating malaria rates across 30 rural Indonesian jungle villages with a goal of testing 150 individuals. Gathering a simple random sample across all 30 villages would force researchers to visit every location, creating massive travel expenses. Using multistage sampling, researchers might randomly select half of the villages ($30 \times 0.5 = 15$ villages) and then randomly select 10 individuals from each of those 15 villages ($15 \times 10 = 150$ individuals). This approach significantly cuts data collection costs while maintaining reliable results.

blocks.title: Figure 1.15
blocks.caption: Examples of cluster and multistage sampling. In the top panel, cluster sampling was used: data were binned into nine clusters, three of these clusters were sampled, and all observations within these three cluster were included in the sample. In the bottom panel, multistage sampling was used, which diﬀers from cluster sampling only in that we randomly select a subset of each cluster to be included in the sample rather than measuring every case in each sampled cluster.
blocks.alt: Figure 1.15: Examples of cluster and multistage sampling. In the top panel, cluster sampling was used: data were binned into nine clusters, three of these clusters were sampled, and all observations within these three cluster were included in the sample. In the bottom panel, multistage sampling was used, which diﬀers from cluster sampling only in that we randomly select a subset of each cluster to be included in the sample rather than measuring every case in each sampled cluster.
blocks.description: Two stacked panels, each showing the same nine labelled circles of dots, Cluster 1 through Cluster 9, scattered across a rectangle. In the top panel three whole clusters, 3, 4 and 8, are outlined with red dashed borders and every dot inside them is circled in red; the other six clusters are untouched. That is cluster sampling: you pick a few groups at random and measure everybody in them. In the bottom panel the same three clusters are outlined in red dashed lines, but only a few dots inside each are circled, the rest left plain. That is multistage sampling: pick a few groups at random, then take a random sample within each chosen group. The point is cost, first and foremost: both designs save you from travelling to all nine clusters, and multistage saves further by not measuring every member of the ones you do visit.

blocks.content: The key insight to remember is that stratified sampling works best when cases within strata are similar, whereas cluster and multistage sampling work best when cases within clusters are diverse.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Stratified sampling divides a population into homogeneous strata to increase precision.
Cluster sampling randomly selects entire clusters and measures every observation within them.
Multistage sampling randomly selects clusters and then takes a random sample within each selected cluster.
Cluster and multistage sampling are often far more economical when studying dispersed populations.
Analyzing data from stratified, cluster, or multistage samples requires more advanced techniques than simple random sampling.

items.term: Classifying Statistical Concepts in Sample Data

blocks.content:
When analyzing data from a large population, collecting information from every individual is often impossible due to time or resource limits. Researchers solve this issue by gathering data from a smaller subset of the population and organizing their findings into specific statistical categories.

To analyze sample data accurately, we must distinguish between four fundamental concepts. An **observation** is a single individual or case in the dataset. A **variable** is a characteristic recorded for each observation. A **sample statistic** is a numerical value calculated directly from the collected sample data. Finally, a **population parameter** is a numerical value that describes the entire target population, which is usually unknown.

Consider an investigation aimed at estimating the proportion of videos on YouTube that feature cats. Because a researcher cannot watch every video on YouTube, they use an automated process to randomly select 1,000 videos. Upon analyzing this subset, the researcher finds that exactly 20 of these videos contain cats.

To compute the sample statistic, the inputs are the number of cat videos in the sample (20) and the total number of videos in the sample (1,000). The researcher divides 20 by 1,000, which yields 0.02, or 2%. In this scenario, a single video in the selected group is an **observation**. The condition of whether a video features a cat or not is the **variable**. The computed figure of 2% represents the **sample statistic**. The true, unknown percentage of all videos on YouTube that feature cats represents the **population parameter**.

The essential insight to remember is that sample statistics are calculated values from collected data used to estimate true, unknown population parameters.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An observation is an individual case or subject sampled from a larger population.
A variable is a specific characteristic measured or recorded for each observation.
A sample statistic is a calculated numerical summary derived directly from sample data.
A population parameter is a numerical summary value representing an entire population.

items.term: Principles of Experimental Design and Bias Reduction

blocks.content:
When researchers want to prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship between variables, observational studies are insufficient because confounding variables can skew results. To solve this problem, researchers conduct **experiments**, where they intentionally assign treatments to study subjects. 

Good experimental design relies on four core principles: **controlling**, **randomization**, **replication**, and **blocking**. Controlling minimizes differences in how subjects are treated, such as ensuring all participants take a medication with exactly 12 ounces of water. Randomization accounts for uncontrollable variables by randomly assigning cases to groups, balancing out hidden differences and avoiding bias. Replication involves using a sufficiently large sample size so that the effect of the explanatory variable can be accurately estimated. Finally, blocking accounts for known variables that influence the response variable. In blocking, subjects are first divided into groups called **blocks** based on a specific characteristic before being randomly assigned to treatment groups.

To see how blocking works in practice, consider a medical trial with 54 patients testing a heart attack drug, as illustrated in Figure 1.16. Researchers suspect patient risk level influences heart attack outcomes. First, they split the 54 patients into two blocks based on risk: 22 low-risk patients and 32 high-risk patients. Next, they randomly split each block exactly in half to form the final study groups. Dividing the 22 low-risk patients in half assigns 11 low-risk patients to the control group and 11 low-risk patients to the treatment group. Dividing the 32 high-risk patients in half assigns 16 high-risk patients to the control group and 16 high-risk patients to the treatment group. Consequently, both the control group and the treatment group contain exactly 27 total patients with identical proportions of low-risk (11) and high-risk (16) individuals.

blocks.title: Figure 1.16
blocks.caption: Blocking using a variable depicting patient risk. Patients are ﬁrst divided into low-risk and high-risk blocks, then each block is evenly separated into the treatment groups using randomization. This strategy ensures an equal representation of patients in each treatment group from both the low-risk and high-risk categories.
blocks.alt: Figure 1.16: Blocking using a variable depicting patient risk. Patients are ﬁrst divided into low-risk and high-risk blocks, then each block is evenly separated into the treatment groups using randomization. This strategy ensures an equal representation of patients in each treatment group from both the low-risk and high-risk categories.
blocks.description: A flow diagram, read top to bottom, of a blocked randomized experiment. At the top a box holds fifty-four numbered patients, drawn as a grid of dots, with two colours mixed together: solid blue dots and open red circles. Arrows labelled "create blocks" split this into two boxes, "Low-risk patients" on the left holding all the open red circles and "High-risk patients" on the right holding all the solid blue dots. From each of those, an arrow labelled "randomly split in half" leads down into two final boxes, "Control" and "Treatment", each of which now receives about half of the low-risk patients and about half of the high-risk patients. The takeaway is the order of operations: block first on the variable you know matters (risk level), then randomize within each block, so the control and treatment groups end up with comparable risk profiles instead of relying on luck to balance them.

blocks.content:
To prevent emotional or psychological expectations from biasing results, studies use a **placebo**—a fake treatment such as a sugar pill. When participants do not know whether they are receiving the real treatment or a placebo, the study is **blind**. To prevent researchers from accidentally giving extra care to treated patients, modern studies use a **double-blind** setup where neither the participants nor the interacting healthcare staff know who receives the active treatment.

The key insight to remember is that randomized experiments, complemented by blocking and double-blind controls, isolate the true effect of an explanatory variable by neutralizing both biological confounding variables and psychological bias.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Randomized experiments allow researchers to establish causal connections between variables by controlling treatment assignments.
The four basic principles of experimental design are controlling, randomization, replication, and blocking.
Blocking groups similar subjects together before randomization to guarantee that confounding characteristics are evenly distributed across treatment groups.
Blinding and placebos prevent psychological bias, while double-blind setups ensure researchers do not treat groups differently.
Replication relies on observing a large enough sample of cases to accurately estimate treatment effects.

blocks.content:
Researchers face a fundamental challenge when testing new treatments: extraneous variables, such as participant age or biological sex, can distort results and mask the true effect of a treatment. To isolate cause-and-effect relationships clearly, statistical experiments rely on careful structural design techniques like controlled treatment allocation and **blocking**.

An experiment begins by separating participants into different experimental groups. The **explanatory variable** (or factor) is the variable being manipulated by researchers, while the **response variable** is the outcome measured at the end of the trial. To prevent background characteristics from skewing results, researchers use **blocking**, which groups similar individuals together before assigning treatments randomly within each group (a **blocking variable**).

Consider a real experiment testing whether chia seeds cause weight loss. Researchers recruited 38 men and 38 women, for a total of 76 participants. To control for potential differences in metabolism between sexes, researchers used biological sex as a **blocking variable**. Within the male block of 38 participants, half (19 men) were randomly assigned to the treatment group (receiving 25 grams of chia seeds twice daily), and the other half (19 men) were assigned to the control group (receiving a placebo). Similarly, within the female block of 38 participants, half (19 women) were randomly assigned to treatment and half (19 women) to control. This design yielded a treatment group of 38 people (19 men and 19 women) and a control group of 38 people (19 men and 19 women).

The core insight of experimental design is that controlling extraneous factors through **blocking** and random assignment ensures that differences in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment itself rather than background variations.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Experimental design controls extraneous factors to establish clear causal connections between variables.
The explanatory variable is manipulated into treatments, while the response variable measures the effect.
Blocking divides subjects into groups based on key characteristics before random treatment assignment occurs.
Placebos and blinding help control for participant and researcher expectations during an experiment.

items.term: Evaluating Study Designs for Generalizability and Causality

blocks.content:
Researchers often want to determine whether a specific treatment causes an outcome, or whether findings from a sample apply to a broader population. A common problem in data analysis is drawing incorrect causal conclusions from observational data, or generalizing sample findings when the sample is biased or non-representative.

To establish causality, researchers must use a **randomized experiment**. In a randomized experiment, participants are randomly assigned to different treatment conditions. This random assignment balances potential confounding factors across groups, allowing researchers to attribute observed differences in outcomes directly to the intervention. In contrast, an **observational study** merely observes individuals without intervening. While observational studies can show associations between variables, they cannot establish causal relationships because confounding variables may influence the results.

To evaluate whether results can be generalized, researchers examine how the sample was selected. **Generalizability** requires a representative sample of the target population, such as a random sample. If participants are self-selected volunteers or if a large portion of the original sample drops out, the remaining group may not represent the population.

Consider a public health study investigating whether fruit and vegetable consumption improves psychological well-being in young adults. Researchers recruited student volunteers at the University of Otago and randomly assigned them to three groups: (1) diet-as-usual, (2) text message reminders plus fruit vouchers, or (3) two additional daily servings of fresh produce. After 14 days, only the third group showed significant improvements in psychological well-being. Because participants were randomly assigned to treatment groups, the study can establish a **causal relationship** between receiving extra produce and improved well-being for those participants. However, because the sample consisted entirely of student volunteers from one university, the results cannot be generalized to all young adults.

The key insight to remember is that random assignment allows for causal conclusions, whereas random sampling enables generalizability to the broader population.
